Text 1 — Article
Collector of Character
Troy Archer started picking through rubbish for ‘old stuff’ when he was
just 10. He's been hooked on that feeling of discovery ever since.
My mum always said I was a fossicker*. I remember pulling the drawers
out at home and looking through them as a kid. There were times I would
visit my uncle, clean his room from top to bottom and put everything
in order. He used to gather all sorts of random stuff and I would sort
everything into categories. Another uncle lived on a farm and they used to
dig holes to dump rubbish. As a 10-year-old I remember digging deep into
the hole and pulling stuff out. I found old tins, newspapers and packaging.
I knew clearly then what I was into — old stuff. I loved the feeling of
discovering something.
I started seriously collecting skateboards when I was 18. I was walking
home after being out all night and went past a garage sale where they had
some old skateboards ... I started gathering other things about five years
ago. I have around 350 skateboards and 500 other bits and pieces.
I now collect industrial things that have character. I've been going to the
tip** forever. I go to the tip shop, op shop or a garage sale every day ...
I love walking in and not knowing what I’m going to see. I don’t always
have to buy things either: I just want to see them.
There are a bunch of guys who also go to the tip and they’ve got as much
character as the things I find. There are around 10 guys I see every day —
they’re between 45 and 75. For some of these guys it’s their business. Like
there are two called Bob and Neil who will recondition stuff and sell it on
at the markets. Then there’s George. He’s about 70 and missing a bunch
of fingers. I’ve never seen him buy anything, he just looks. Maybe these
old things connect him back with his youth .
Text 1 continues on page 3
Text 1 (continued)
I'm a graphic artist by trade, so for me it’s all about the compositions,
typography and colours. And I like things to be unique. Old things are all
unique. They're decrepit*** in their own way.
Ihave a little studio set up in my garage and shoot photos of everything I
collect. I like how the size of things becomes irrelevant. I’ve got all these
old plastic toys and they’re only small, but when you shoot them they can
look big. Or I could shoot a tyre or trunk and it looks the same size as the
little plastic toys.
... If could do anything with my collection, I would open a space that
allows all of it to be shown and bought. It could go on to have its own life
and I could buy more stuff.
I'm just starting to work out why I’m attracted to this kind of thing. Part
of it is the fragility of life and how you get old, pass on and leave your
legacy. When I find something that is one shade off being done for good
and I bring it back, it feels like I’m giving something a new life.
Louise

Text 3 — Fiction extract
... the weather had turned bad, with squalls coming in from the sea, but
under the overhang of the cliffs someone found enough dry driftwood to
keep a fire going. I was sitting off to one side, watching, and even after
midnight I could still see the others, lying around on blankets, smoking,
and poking sticks into the flames. I could hear their voices too, carried on
the wind. They were telling horror stories ...
With the wind moaning up off the night sea the way it did, and the
shadows from the flames moving among the rocks, I felt my skin crawl,
and the goose flesh come up on the insides of my arms. I couldn’t help
thinking that just under the skin, even on me, pale as I was, veins ran with
red blood ... but then a kid called Nigel Kratzman, who lived next to me
at the time, started talking about trucks—his favourite subject—and since
that didn’t interest me, and I was just getting over a cold, I thought I'd
better slip away and get some sleep.
None of the others saw me move; I was in the dark, well outside the bright
ring of firelight.
That afternoon, when the rain came, all the sleeping gear had been shifted
into a cliff cave, behind the fire. It was high in there, going right up into
the cliff itself, but the entrance was almost sealed by sand and I had to
drop on my hands and knees to crawl in.
... I made sure I could still see outside from where I was lying, to watch
the others around the fire ...
The cave disappeared into even deeper darkness behind me, and I was
feeling queer about that, so I got out of my sleeping bag and shifted it over
against a side wall—but I could still see the light of the fire.
... was like that when the others came in. They fooled around for a while
then started to quieten down. The fire burned low and the coals glowed
strongly sometimes, then died right away at others. That was the wind,
rising and falling. I remember lying there with my eyes so wide open,
staring out, that they went dry and I made myself blink to wet them.
I couldn’t help feeling there was something wrong about that place.
At some time I must have dozed off because my back pack slipped down
and what started everything was when my head fell back against the
rock—but no rock ever sounded like that—a dull gonging sound, deep,
not loud, like the echo in an empty fuel drum after it’s been kicked.
Text 3 continues on page 6
Text 3 (continued)
I did not move a muscle. I lay there thinking someone was behind me, in
that darkness. But nothing happened. No movement. No voice. I started
to count in my head. Ten. Twenty. Thirty. Forty. Still nothing, even after
I passed a hundred. Then I lifted up my hands, back up together, without
moving my head or the rest of my body, and my fingers touched stuff like
hair—fine and wiry—and beyond that, something cold and hard.
I pulled my hands back and reached for my torch, then I rolled on my
stomach so I could see. Almost right in front of my face was a web of
hairy roots that hung down from the blackness, from the cave ceiling I
guess. When I pushed the roots away I could see what looked like the
sides of a smooth black rock or boulder, but when I touched it and rapped
it this thing was a big pot, on a ledge of rock in the cave wall—a big metal
pot.
... [got up on my knees and crawled out of my sleeping bag but I didn’t
say anything. I shone my torch around the top of the pot and there was a
lid with a handle on it. Dirt and small rocks were all over this. The lid had
a lot of weight as if there was suction from inside. I yanked hard, pulling
back with my body, and the lid came away, sliding towards me about 3 or
4 centimetres. Kneeling up on the ledge, I got above the thing and shone
my torch down into the gap but the stink coming out was terrible. A hot,
musty smell.
I pulled my head back and must have made some sound because then I
heard the others talking and saw torches flashing around the roof of the
cave. Someone had spotted me on the ledge.
I didn’t care that they were watching me. I really wanted to see what
was inside that pot and pushed the lid back a bit more so I could look in
without getting too close. I could see a rectangular shape, or a corner of a
rectangular shape—and another thing—I couldn’t make out what it was.
... [put my hand inside and groped about. The thing I touched was stiff
with a rough sort of surface that felt like dry leather. I remember thinking
this could be anything and I would have to wash my hands later, then I
picked it up between two fingers and lifted it out. Everyone saw what it
was as it came over the edge of the pot, and straight away I chucked it
down onto my sleeping bag. It was a human hand.
Gary CREW
from Strange Objects
